items.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot Flaw Lets Attackers Gain Elevated Privileges Without User Interaction
items.summary: Microsoft disclosed a critical Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that could let an attacker with limited privileges gain higher permissions over a network without any action from another user. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-50691, was released on November 19, 2026, and received a CVSS 3.1 base score of 9.9 out of 10. Microsoft says customers do not need to take any action to resolve it. Microsoft 365 Copilot Flaw The distinction is that no user interaction does not mean no initial access. The attacker needs some permissions before exploiting the flaw, but does not need another user to click a link, open a file, or approve a request. That separates this issue from SearchLeak, a one-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that Cyber Security News covered in June. Microsoft classified the weakness as improper authorization, or CWE-285. Authorization is the check that decides what someone can do after the service knows who they are. When that check is missing or applied incorrectly, a user can gain access to a resource or action that their existing permissions should block. Microsoft’s assessment describes a network-reachable flaw with low attack complexity. It also rates the potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability as high. In plain terms, a successful attack could put protected data, its accuracy, and access to affected resources at risk. The score also reflects a change in scope, meaning the impact could extend beyond the security boundary of the affected component. These ratings describe potential impact, not confirmed customer harm. Microsoft’s assessment listed the flaw as not exploited at publication. The Microsoft Security Response Center advisory says no customer action is required, so administrators do not need to install a local update for this CVE. This flaw is separate from EchoLeak , an earlier Copilot issue that could expose information without user interaction and did not require an attacker to have prior access. Here, the reported impact is higher privileges for an attacker who already has limited access. The update does not eliminate the necessity of reviewing existing permissions. Microsoft’s Copilot security guidance advises checking SharePoint sites for files shared too broadly and restricting access to only those who need it. This review addresses a separate risk: even if Copilot enforces permissions accurately, it can still make files easier to find for users who already have more access than intended. items.title: Critical N-able Mail Assure SSRF Vulnerability Allows Attackers to Reach Internal Systems via LDAP Sync
items.summary: N-able has patched a critical vulnerability in MailAssure, also known as SpamExperts, that lets an attacker with privileged API access reach internal network services through the email security platform. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. N-able’s November 22 security advisory identifies build 20261121.1943 as the fix and lists all earlier builds as affected. N-able Mail Assure SSRF Vulnerability The disclosure follows a November 16 service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the N-able server breach , the company confirmed unauthorized access to one hosted server and disabled management access while it responded. Dashboard and API access returned late on November 21. The advisory does not establish how the attacker first gained access to the hosted environment. The flaw affects a connection check that MailAssure runs for LDAP synchronization when a mail relay is configured. As N-able’s LDAP mailbox sync guide explains, LDAP, short for Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, lets MailAssure query an organization’s directory and keep its mailbox and alias lists up to date. The problem was not with LDAP itself. MailAssure failed to limit where its server could connect during the check. That makes the flaw a server-side request forgery, or SSRF, classified as CWE-918. A user with the required API privileges can make the MailAssure server connect to internal hosts and ports, learn which services are reachable, and send specially prepared data to them. The distinction matters: internal services do not need to be exposed to the internet for the MailAssure server to reach them. The risk is similar to that described in Cyber Security News’ coverage of the Zimbra SSRF vulnerability : a trusted server can reach systems that an outside user cannot contact directly. In this case, the severity rating specifies that high privileges are required, but no other user needs to take action. N-able’s advisory describes internal network access, not remote code execution. Organizations running MailAssure or SpamExperts should verify that their service is on build 20261121.1943 or later. Customers who cannot check the build themselves should ask their provider to confirm that the fix is in place. The National Vulnerability Database entry records the flaw, which CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 23. Administrators should review who holds privileged API credentials and check available logs for unexpected relay changes or connections from MailAssure to systems outside its normal directory setup. The patch closes the vulnerable connection check, but it cannot show whether someone misused it beforehand. Hosted customers without access to those logs may need help from their provider. items.title: Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
items.summary: CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter's directory service, rated 9.8 out of 10. An attacker who can reach vCenter on the network can become administrator@vsphere.local without a password. A suspected China-nexus espionage group, ARMORY CASTLE, exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom patched it on Nov. 19, and CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Nov. 23 to fix it. Install the patch today. Then plan for the harder job. If anything that could reach your vCenter was compromised at any point since September, the patch closes the door but doesn't take back what went through it. In the intrusion researchers investigated, that included vCenter's SAML signing key, its master encryption key and Active Directory credentials copied straight out of virtual machine disks. Let's see how the attackers used this flaw, which builds fix it, and the hunting and credential rotation that should follow the patch. What Is CVE-2026-123890 Broadcom disclosed the flaw last week, in advisory VMSA-2026-0009 , which fixes five vulnerabilities across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. CVE-2026-123890 is the critical one. An authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service, the component behind vCenter's single sign-on. Mandiant found it and reported it privately. The bug lives in a remote procedure call interface that vCenter's directory service exposes on TCP port 2012. Its Secure Remote Password login generates predictable identifiers based on timestamps, and according to researchers, an attacker can use that to recover the shared session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local , the most powerful account in a vSphere environment. From there, an attacker can run commands and copy files through the directory service, including data.mdb , the database that holds the SSO domain's accounts and the private key vCenter uses to sign SAML login tokens. It is not a virtual machine escape. It's worse in a different way - it hands over the console that manages every host and VM. Two things make it easy to get wrong: It's a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, the vCenter authentication bypass Broadcom fixed in July. Mandiant observed attackers using CVE-2026-123890 against a vCenter that was already patched for the July flaw. There is no workaround. Broadcom's only fix is the update, which its own FAQ treats as an emergency change. How ARMORY CASTLE used it from a support box to domain credentials Mandiant's write-up shows why vCenter being reachable only from the internal network didn't protect it. The attackers never touched vCenter from the internet. They worked their way to it from the inside. ARMORY CASTLE's path from a remote-support appliance to Active Directory credentials Break in at the edge. The group, formerly tracked as UNC5221, first exploited a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVE-2026-102764. Find the VMware estate. From the support appliance, it scanned the internal network for VMware ports, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080, then moved to internal Linux appliances that had no endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. It dropped two web shells and became root by setting the SUID bit on /bin/env with the gdb debugger. Take vCenter. A custom Go tool Mandiant calls BONESAW exploited CVE-2026-123890 over port 2012, created a new SSO administrator account, copied the directory database and extracted the token-signing key. Forge logins. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to sign SAML tokens as the administrator, a "Golden SAML" attack that bypasses passwords and MFA. Drop into the appliance. The group switched on SSH through vCenter's appliance management API, logged in with its new account, stole vCenter's master encryption key and its PostgreSQL database password, then switched SSH off again. Reach the hosts and the domain. It logged in to ESXi hosts as vpxuser and root, added its own SSH key, and used a Python tool to extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) and registry hives straight from a virtual machine's disk. The files left through the original support appliance. Two backdoors kept the door open: BEARBONES, a modified Dropbear SSH server that accepts a hardcoded password, and LAZYBONES, which takes commands through Slack. The timing matters too. BONESAW's build timestamp is July 13, 2026, and the attackers used it in early September. Go build timestamps can be faked, but Mandiant reads it as a tool built for broader operations, not a one-off. Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890? Product line Affected Fixed in vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.1 9.1.x 9.1.1.0200 vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.0 9.0.x 9.0.2.0200 vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.x 5.2.5 vCenter Server 7.0 7.0 No public fix; extended-support customers go through Broadcom Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure Listed versions See Broadcom KB463116 A few details that trip people up: Patched in July doesn't mean patched now. Every vCenter below the builds in the table needs this update, including systems that already have the CVE-2026-59309 fix. vCenter 7.0 is the hard case. vSphere 7.0 reached the end of general support on Oct. 2, 2025, so there's no public fix. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ also says to presume versions 6.5 and 6.7 are affected. If you're on any of these, restricting network access to port 2012 is your main protection until you can upgrade or obtain a fix. ESXi isn't in the advisory. The flaw is in vCenter. ESXi hosts still matter for the cleanup, because the attackers used vCenter to reach them. Don't run the GitHub "proof of concept." A repository that appeared on Nov. 20 claiming exploit code describes the wrong advisory and fixed versions. As of Nov. 21, Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module titled as an authentication bypass to root, so expect working public exploit code soon, if it isn't out already. Why patching isn't enough The patch fixes the login flaw. It does nothing about what an attacker took while the flaw was open, and in this case the stolen items are exactly the kind that keep working: The token-signing key. Anyone holding vCenter's SAML signing key can mint valid administrator logins until that certificate is replaced. A patched vCenter will accept them. New accounts. The attackers created an SSO administrator named sps- followed by random characters in vsphere.local. BONESAW can also add a machine account and grant Global Administrator rights on the vCenter root folder. Appliance secrets. vCenter's master encryption key and PostgreSQL password were copied over SSH. Host access. An SSH key was added to the ESXi root account. Active Directory. A copy of NTDS.dit plus the SYSTEM hive is enough to recover the password hashes of every account in the domain, offline. The exposure window also runs further back than most patch plans assume. Exploitation started in early September, more than 10 weeks before the fix. If any system that could reach your vCenter's management ports was compromised in that time, treat vCenter as possibly compromised too until you've checked. After the patch: what to hunt for Search logs back to at least early September 2026. These come from Mandiant's analysis; ARMORY CASTLE deletes its tools after use, so absence of files doesn't prove absence of compromise. On the network Connections to TCP 2012 on vCenter from anything other than your documented management hosts, especially Linux appliances or remote-support servers. Internal scans for VMware ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080. Servers calling the Slack API, and SSH services announcing the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, often on high, non-standard ports. Traffic to the 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs in GTIG's report, such as 103.147.251[.]5 and 176.9.89[.]66. On vCenter SSO accounts you didn't create, especially names starting with sps- in vsphere.local, and unexpected members of the Administrators group. A PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh call to the appliance management API, particularly SSH being enabled and disabled again shortly after. SSH logins to the appliance, and reads of the master key or PostgreSQL password files. On ESXi hosts ESXi Host Client logins as vpxuser and root SSH sessions you can't explain. New entries in root's authorized_keys. Hidden directories such as .a on VMFS volumes, and the files vmfs-pydist.tar.gz or vmfs_browser.py. On internal Linux appliances The files /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), /tmp/123.key and /tmp/gdb_file. /usr/bin/vmtoolscs (LAZYBONES) running as a systemd service that restarts every 50 minutes. Web shells named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp, and the SUID bit set on /bin/env. GTIG has published YARA rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES and both web shells in the same report. After the patch: what to rotate and reset If you find signs of compromise, or can't rule it out because logs don't reach back to September, work through this in order. Patch and lock down access first, or the attacker can simply take the new secrets too. These steps reflect the consensus among incident responders building on Mandiant's findings; follow Broadcom's knowledge base procedures for each vCenter task. Patch, then close the paths in. Install the fixed build, patch BeyondTrust Remote Support if you run it, and restrict ports 2012, 443, 5480 and 22 on vCenter to named management hosts. Rebuild what you can't trust. Where compromise is confirmed, rebuild vCenter and the affected Linux appliances rather than cleaning them. The attackers had root and deleted their tools as they went. Replace the STS signing certificate. This is the step that kills forged SAML tokens, and no other step does. Plan for the knock-on effect: products that trust vCenter single sign-on may need to be re-registered. Afterwards, confirm that sessions created with the old key fail. Reset vSphere identities. Reset administrator@vsphere.local and every other SSO and local account, remove accounts and Administrators-group members you didn't create, and rotate solution-user certificates, service-account passwords and third-party integration tokens tied to vsphere.local. Clean up the hosts. Reset ESXi root passwords and remove any SSH keys you didn't add to authorized_keys. Treat Active Directory as exposed if a domain controller ran there. If a domain controller's virtual disk sat on a host the attackers reached, assume every domain password hash was taken. That means resetting privileged and service accounts and resetting the krbtgt account twice, with time for replication in between, the standard response to a stolen NTDS.dit. Step 6 is the one that turns a VMware incident into a company-wide one, so decide early whether it applies to you. Harden the vCenter control plane This is ARMORY CASTLE's second zero-day in one intrusion, and Mandiant's point is that patching alone can't keep up with that. Its hardening advice centers on making vCenter hard to reach and noisy when someone tries. Don't rely on the built-in appliance firewall. Mandiant notes that the firewall managed through vCenter's appliance management interface can't restrict access port by port, so trusting a backup server for the API trusts it for SSH and management too. It's managed from the same interface an attacker would take over, it doesn't log blocked connections remotely, and it doesn't control outbound traffic. Enforce rules below the application. Mandiant recommends its VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool, which applies default-deny iptables rules at the operating-system level, filters outbound traffic and forwards blocked connections and shell commands to a SIEM. By Mandiant's analysis, those rules would have blocked the exploit on port 2012, the forged logins on 443, the SSH pivot and the Slack command channel. Test any such rules under change control before production. Close the visibility gaps. The attackers chose Linux appliances with no EDR as their staging ground. Inventory every appliance that can reach vCenter or ESXi, and get logs off them if you can't run an agent. Manage vSphere only from privileged access workstations, as set out in Mandiant's vSphere defender's guide. Frequently asked questions What is CVE-2026-123890? An attacker with network access to vCenter's TCP port 2012 can obtain an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local without a password. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 20, 2026, with a Nov. 23 remediation deadline for federal agencies. There is no workaround. I installed the July fix for CVE-2026-59309. Am I protected? No. CVE-2026-123890 is a separate flaw, and Mandiant observed it being exploited against a vCenter already patched for CVE-2026-59309. You need the November builds. Search logs back to at least early September 2026. These come from Mandiant's analysis; ARMORY CASTLE deletes its tools after use, so absence of files doesn't prove absence of compromise.

On the network

  • Connections to TCP 2012 on vCenter from anything other than your documented management hosts, especially Linux appliances or remote-support servers.

  • Internal scans for VMware ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080.

  • Servers calling the Slack API, and SSH services announcing the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, often on high, non-standard ports.

  • Traffic to the 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs in GTIG's report, such as 103.147.251[.]5 and 176.9.89[.]66.

On vCenter

  • SSO accounts you didn't create, especially names starting with sps- in vsphere.local, and unexpected members of the Administrators group.

  • A PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh call to the appliance management API, particularly SSH being enabled and disabled again shortly after.

  • SSH logins to the appliance, and reads of the master key or PostgreSQL password files.

On ESXi hosts

  • ESXi Host Client logins as vpxuser and root SSH sessions you can't explain.

  • New entries in root's authorized_keys.

  • Hidden directories such as .a on VMFS volumes, and the files vmfs-pydist.tar.gz or vmfs_browser.py.

On internal Linux appliances

  • The files /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), /tmp/123.key and /tmp/gdb_file.

  • /usr/bin/vmtoolscs (LAZYBONES) running as a systemd service that restarts every 50 minutes.

  • Web shells named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp, and the SUID bit set on /bin/env.

GTIG has published YARA rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES and both web shells in the same report.

After the patch: what to rotate and reset

If you find signs of compromise, or can't rule it out because logs don't reach back to September, work through this in order. Patch and lock down access first, or the attacker can simply take the new secrets too. These steps reflect the consensus among incident responders building on Mandiant's findings; follow Broadcom's knowledge base procedures for each vCenter task.

  1. Patch, then close the paths in. Install the fixed build, patch BeyondTrust Remote Support if you run it, and restrict ports 2012, 443, 5480 and 22 on vCenter to named management hosts.

  2. Rebuild what you can't trust. Where compromise is confirmed, rebuild vCenter and the affected Linux appliances rather than cleaning them. The attackers had root and deleted their tools as they went.

  3. Replace the STS signing certificate. This is the step that kills forged SAML tokens, and no other step does. Plan for the knock-on effect: products that trust vCenter single sign-on may need to be re-registered. Afterwards, confirm that sessions created with the old key fail.

  4. Reset vSphere identities. Reset administrator@vsphere.local and every other SSO and local account, remove accounts and Administrators-group members you didn't create, and rotate solution-user certificates, service-account passwords and third-party integration tokens tied to vsphere.local.

  5. Clean up the hosts. Reset ESXi root passwords and remove any SSH keys you didn't add to authorized_keys.

  6. Treat Active Directory as exposed if a domain controller ran there. If a domain controller's virtual disk sat on a host the attackers reached, assume every domain password hash was taken. That means resetting privileged and service accounts and resetting the krbtgt account twice, with time for replication in between, the standard response to a stolen NTDS.dit.

Step 6 is the one that turns a VMware incident into a company-wide one, so decide early whether it applies to you.

Harden the vCenter control plane

This is ARMORY CASTLE's second zero-day in one intrusion, and Mandiant's point is that patching alone can't keep up with that. Its hardening advice centers on making vCenter hard to reach and noisy when someone tries.

Don't rely on the built-in appliance firewall. Mandiant notes that the firewall managed through vCenter's appliance management interface can't restrict access port by port, so trusting a backup server for the API trusts it for SSH and management too. It's managed from the same interface an attacker would take over, it doesn't log blocked connections remotely, and it doesn't control outbound traffic.

Enforce rules below the application. Mandiant recommends its VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool, which applies default-deny iptables rules at the operating-system level, filters outbound traffic and forwards blocked connections and shell commands to a SIEM. By Mandiant's analysis, those rules would have blocked the exploit on port 2012, the forged logins on 443, the SSH pivot and the Slack command channel. Test any such rules under change control before production.

Close the visibility gaps. The attackers chose Linux appliances with no EDR as their staging ground. Inventory every appliance that can reach vCenter or ESXi, and get logs off them if you can't run an agent. Manage vSphere only from privileged access workstations, as set out in Mandiant's vSphere defender's guide.

Frequently asked questions

What is CVE-2026-123890?

CVE-2026-123890 is a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter Server. An attacker with network access to vCenter's TCP port 2012 can obtain an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local without a password. Broadcom fixed it on Nov. 19, 2026, in VMSA-2026-0009.

Is CVE-2026-123890 being exploited?

Yes. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 20, 2026, with a Nov. 23 remediation deadline for federal agencies.

Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890?

vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m, and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix; extended-support customers must go through Broadcom. There is no workaround.

I installed the July fix for CVE-2026-59309. Am I protected?

No. CVE-2026-123890 is a separate flaw, and Mandiant observed it being exploited against a vCenter already patched for CVE-2026-59309. You need the November builds.

Is there a public exploit for CVE-2026-123890?

As of Nov. 21, 2026, the attackers' tool hadn't been released, and a GitHub repository claiming a proof of concept was fake. Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module, so working public exploit code is expected soon.

Is CVE-2026-123890 a VM escape? Do I need to patch ESXi?

No on both counts. The flaw is in vCenter, and ESXi isn't listed in the advisory. But an attacker who controls vCenter can reach every ESXi host it manages, so check your hosts during cleanup.

Know which flaws are being used before the advisory lands

CVE-2026-123890 was exploited for more than 10 weeks before it was disclosed, and it was reached through a second zero-day in a remote-support appliance. Defenders can't patch what hasn't been disclosed, but they can know which of their exposed systems sit in an attacker's path and act within hours when exploitation becomes public.

items.summary: An attacker using the CyberStrikeAI framework gained access to 3,392 user accounts and their active session tokens during a four-day cloud intrusion in October 2026. The operator also decrypted a bastion host’s database to recover 50 SSH private keys. The activity spanned two Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts and seven Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) clusters, according to a November 23 disclosure. The scale became clear only after investigators compared the victim’s security logs with more than 3,000 files left exposed on the attacker’s server. The logs showed activity inside AWS and Kubernetes, while the exposed files revealed what happened in the identity system and on other hosts. A separate investigation into exposed ARTEX operator servers showed how similar mistakes have helped researchers reconstruct AI-assisted attacks. Researchers at Wiz identified a custom rootkit, malware designed to hide and maintain access, on compromised Kubernetes nodes. It masqueraded as a font configuration service and used DNS traffic to communicate. The sample had zero detections on VirusTotal at the time Wiz examined it, but the public report did not disclose a file hash that defenders could use to identify it. AI-Powered Hackers Gain Access to 3,392 User Accounts The intruder entered with a stolen session tied to a Terraform runner, a service used to manage cloud infrastructure. That access led to elevated Kubernetes privileges. Wiz also documented a compromise of the Jenkins build controller and the use of stolen cloud credentials from the attacker’s own server. Those credentials exposed infrastructure records and cloud secrets beyond the systems where they were originally issued. The attacker’s files showed that forged administrator tokens opened access to the identity provider’s 3,392 users and their live session tokens. The tokens matter because they can let someone act as an already signed-in user without knowing the password. The figure describes the accounts the attacker could access; the report does not say the operator individually signed in as all 3,392 users. The operator decrypted the database of a bastion host, a controlled entry point for administrators connecting to private systems, and recovered 50 SSH private keys. Artex harvester agentic attacks walkthrough (Source – Wiz) The files also showed that the attacker placed beacons, which can signal back to an operator, on 19 hosts. Wiz did not say that each recovered key was used or that the 50 keys corresponded to 50 separate machines. The breach also reached the systems that build and deploy software. The attacker extracted GitHub Actions secrets and changed the production Jenkins configuration to run before its approval check, exposing production secrets. Separate reporting on GitHub Actions credential theft shows why build systems are valuable targets: a single workflow can have access to credentials for several services. Wiz also found that the operator collected Anthropic API keys from 50 hosts and searched employees’ AI coding-assistant histories for production sign-on credentials. CyberStrikeAI as the framework The original Wiz Research report identifies CyberStrikeAI as the framework that ran the operation. Investigators found a copy of ARTEX on the same server, but that does not make the intrusion part of the same campaign as the other attacks discussed in the report. Seeing both sides of an attack (Source – Wiz) Wiz also noted csai-escape , csai-pentest-role , and csai-probe as names the operator left on resources in this case. Those strings can help narrow a search, but they are not unique fingerprints. In a separate campaign, Wiz saw more than 220 proxy IPs used against a single target. That churn helps explain why FBI guidance on ARTEX is more useful alongside behavioral monitoring than as a reason to rely on static blocklists. For defenders, the strongest leads are unusual administrative sessions, sudden spikes in secret retrieval, and cloud credentials used from unexpected locations. If the logs confirm exposure, invalidate affected sessions and replace the stolen SSH keys and other secrets. Then review which systems still trust those keys, which build jobs can reach production, and whether any workloads gained privileges they did not need. A password reset alone does not address a stolen SSH key or a compromised build credential. items.title: Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins to Steal Passwords and Take Over Websites
items.summary: Hackers planted a remote-control backdoor in nine versions of six WordPress plugins from WP connect on November 22, 2026. The malware could let an attacker steal password hashes, run commands, and take over a website. But WordPress.org blocked the tainted versions before distributing them and closed all six plugins that evening. The advisory does not report confirmed password theft or website takeovers from the incident. Wordfence estimated that the six plugins had more than 3,600 active installations combined. That figure describes the plugins’ reach, not the number of compromised sites. The malicious versions were committed through the developer’s own WordPress.org account. WP connect reported that its account had been compromised, but how the attackers gained access was not clear when the advisory was published. Researchers at Wordfence identified the malware independently of the WordPress.org Plugins Team. Wordfence’s PRISM monitoring system flagged suspicious changes in two plugins within a minute of each other, and analysts traced the same module to four more. A researcher known as Computeronfire separately reported the backdoor in Air WP Sync. Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins The affected releases were Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress 2.9.1–2.9.4, WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress 1.7.4, Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms 2.6.3, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable 2.5.4, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion 1.6.4, and Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce 1.0.2. The release immediately preceding each plugin’s affected version or range did not contain the backdoor. Each tainted release loaded a new PHP file that passed itself off as an analytics and update module. An earlier WordPress plugin backdoor case also hid malicious code behind an update-related feature. In the WP connect incident, Wordfence found the same module across all six plugins, with a slightly earlier draft in Air WP Sync 2.9.1. The module ran during normal site requests and used WP-Cron, WordPress’s scheduler, to check in every 30 minutes as a fallback. It sent the site URL, software versions, server account name, and previous command output to a remote server. The module could execute PHP sent back by that server without a WordPress login. It also disabled verification of the server’s TLS certificate. Backdoor offers multiple capabilities The backdoor could run shell commands, read or change files, query database tables, and extract usernames, email addresses, and password hashes. A hash is not a plaintext password, but a stolen hash can be used to test password guesses offline. The malware could also plant a webshell, a script that provides remote access, or set up an hourly task to run malicious code. As earlier reporting on self-rebuilding WordPress backdoors showed, removing the original plugin does not necessarily remove everything it installed. WordPress.org’s release hold kept the versions out of the update channel while Gandalf, its automated reviewer, independently detected the malicious code and stopped the rollout. The incident shows why automated plugin update reviews matter even when a commit comes from a trusted developer account. Wordfence tracks the backdoor as CVE-2026-135202, with a critical CVSS score of 9.8. No patched versions were available at disclosure. items.title: Critical Bluetooth Flaw Could Let Hackers Take Control of Trailer Brakes While Driving
items.summary: A critical Bluetooth flaw in Elecbrakes trailer brake controllers could let someone nearby apply, adjust, or release a trailer’s brakes while it is being towed. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-96805, carries a 9.6 severity score. It requires no pairing, PIN, or action from the driver. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency disclosed the issue on November 19, 2026, alongside two related vulnerabilities. Firmware fixes are available for the EB2 and VM1, but owners must start the update themselves in the Elecbrakes app. The older ELBC 2000 also has the flaw and had no fix at disclosure. The distinction matters because a trailer brake controller governs how much braking force the trailer applies, not how the tow vehicle’s own brakes operate. Element Digital researchers Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy identified the vulnerabilities after Forck noticed his in-car remote had connected to someone else’s trailer without a pairing prompt. They tested only equipment they owned, on private property or in a closed setup. Their report describes a product vulnerability, not a malware campaign. Critical Bluetooth Flaw The controller uses Bluetooth Low Energy to communicate with the Elecbrakes app and wireless remote. On vulnerable firmware, the controller did not verify that braking instructions came from an authorized device. Unlike the PerfektBlue automotive Bluetooth flaws , which affected infotainment software, the Elecbrakes flaw directly exposed a function that controls braking force. In controlled driving tests, stronger unauthorized braking produced noticeably greater deceleration than lighter braking at the same speed. On a public road, unexpected trailer braking could upset the balance of the tow vehicle and trailer. Earlier reporting on a wireless train braking flaw describes a separate technology but highlights the same safety principle: a brake controller must verify who is giving it instructions. The second critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-125273, concerns replay: a controller could accept a previously issued instruction again without checking whether it was fresh. The test setup (Source – Element Digital) It also scored 9.6. That differs from the Volkswagen Bluetooth hacking demonstration , where researchers exploited infotainment software to access cabin functions and data rather than directly commanding trailer brakes. The third issue, CVE-2026-124281, scored 6.1 and affects the wireless firmware update channel. CISA warned that inadequate protection could allow unauthorized firmware changes. The researchers did not install modified firmware on a live controller, so the potential for lasting changes should not be confused with the brake activation they demonstrated in controlled testing. Firmware Fixes and What Elecbrakes Owners Should Do Elecbrakes received the report on May 18 and released fixes on July 6. The CISA industrial control advisory directs EB2 owners to install firmware 3.0.4.4.3 or later and VM1 owners to install 1.3.4.2.1 or later. Open the Elecbrakes app, connect to the controller, and check the installed version. If it is older, start the update manually rather than assuming it has already installed. The patched controllers restrict braking and access to update mode to an authenticated connection. Initial pairing requires physical confirmation through the tow vehicle’s brake pedal. The change made older wireless remotes incompatible with the new pairing process, so Elecbrakes offered affected EB2 and VM1 owners free replacement remotes. Owners who use a remote should check whether theirs needs replacing. All versions of the ELBC 2000 were listed as affected, with no firmware fix available at disclosure. As earlier reporting on legacy Renault vehicle software illustrates, equipment can remain in use long after its software ages. ELBC 2000 owners should contact Elecbrakes for model-specific guidance and check the app periodically for a remediation update. The manual update also leaves a gap between releasing a fix and protecting trailers on the road. By late October, Elecbrakes told the researchers that about 60% of daily active EB2 and VM1 users had installed the latest firmware. That figure does not account for owners who rarely open the app. Fleet operators should verify the firmware on each controller rather than using that rollout figure as evidence that their own units are patched. items.title: SplitSecure Launches New Access Control Architecture for Humans and AI Agents
items.summary: San Francisco, United States, November 23rd, 2026, CyberNewswire SplitSecure , the cybersecurity technology provider, today unveiled a new access control platform based on secret splitting technology. The platform is intended to replace traditional access controls tools such as password managers, PAM, and vaults. On launch, it supports passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML & OIDC federation, SSH, x.509 CA, OpenPGP, code signing (Nitro, Google Chrome Extensions), and general secrets vaulting. The platform is intended for secure organizations of all sizes, including both large enterprise plans and a free plan for teams of up to six. The access control space today contains a wide variety of tools. A secure organization would typically require a password manager, MFA app, vault, certificate manager, and PAM, among other tools. But despite their variety, all these tools use a common architecture where clients’ secrets are stored in a singular “vault”. It is this architecture SplitSecure seeks to disrupt, with a new way of storing and using secrets based on secret-splitting. Secret splitting is the practice of breaking secrets across multiple devices rather than storing them in one location. This has been common practice in classified government environments for over thirty years but has historically been seen as high-effort and has had only limited adoption in industry. SplitSecure’s new platform is a significant advance of the state of the art, offering a ready-to-use implementation of techniques that were previously limited to advanced security teams in elite organizations. Because of this general advancement, SplitSecure is able to replicate the functionality of many common tools. Its new platform provides password management, MFA, vaulting, certificate signing, and more PAM functionality such as shared accounts and resources. Supported resource types include passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML 2.0 sign-ons, secrets, certificates, SSH certificates, signing keys, OpenPGP identities, and crypto wallets. This new technology also offers the particular advantage that it cryptographically guarantees the service provider has no access to client’s secrets. This is in contrast to traditional PAM tools, in which the provider holds the “keys to the kingdom” at all times and a compromised vendor may be able to compromise client information. Tristan Morris, CEO of SplitSecure, commented: “We were very ambitious […] we wanted a tool where people didn’t have to trust us as the provider, whereby design they’re the custodians of their own secrets. But we also wanted it to be so easy to use you could imagine a non-technical person using it instead of a password manager. We’ve done that, and it’s amazing to see it launch.”He also noted that SplitSecure’s new platform integrates with common identity providers for an easier transition. “It should always be easy to set up,” he said. “Migration, first time setup, our goal was for that to take under half an hour.” Details on supported security and privacy frameworks are available in the SplitSecure Trust Center. The free plan of SplitSecure’s new platform, which is available to all customers now, offers access control with the following key differentiators: Modern Privileged Access: Zero trust, just-in-time access, zero standing privilege, on-demand step-up authentication, multi-party approvals, and quantum resistance come as standard. Condenses Multiple Tools: SplitSecure can condense two to five tools in the security stack. No-Vendor-Threat Architecture: Root keys are held exclusively by the customer, so SplitSecure as the vendor has no access to customer secrets. Built-In Audit and Compliance: Every privileged action are logged automatically with full context on every plan. Paid plans can view the logs for security analysis and forensics. About SplitSecure SplitSecure is a cybersecurity technology provider, established to develop and modernize secret splitting technology. After being founded in 2025 by Tristan Morris and Marc Tremblay, it raised $4.7M from Cowboy, Twelve Below, and Cofound Ventures. Its access control platform combines PAM, password and passkey management, secrets vaulting, and auditing in one product, with root keys held exclusively by the customer. SplitSecure’s new access control platform is free for teams of up to six. Learn more at splitsecure.com or read the documentation . Email: contact@splitsecure.com Website: splitsecure.com Contact Chief of Staff Slava Pashchenko SplitSecure slava@splitsecure.com

items.title: Critical Node.js simple-git Library Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks
items.summary: A critical flaw in simple-git, a popular Node.js library for running Git commands, can let attackers run their own commands on a server. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-134815. It affects apps that pass untrusted input into Git arguments. The National Vulnerability Database says simple-git versions before 4.1.0 contain an argument injection weakness, listed as CWE-88. In plain terms, the library does not properly separate user-supplied text from the options it sends to Git. VulnCheck, which assigned the CVE, rated it 9.2 (Critical) on the CVSS 4.0 scale. The library has a safety guard named allowUnsafePack. It is meant to block dangerous options that make Git run an outside program. Before this fix, the guard only blocked the –exec option for push operations. Attackers can bypass it by adding –exec to other Git actions. Node.js simple-git Library Flaw The risk starts when an application lets outside input reach the listRemote() or raw() functions. An attacker who controls those arguments can slip in –exec for ls-remote, archive, fetch-pack or send-pack. Git then treats the value as the name of a remote program and runs it on the host. The result is remote code execution, which means the attacker’s commands run with the same rights as the Node.js process. The CVSS vector shows the attack needs no login and no user interaction. It also lists high attack complexity and an attack requirement, so a vulnerable app must be set up in a specific way. Even so, the impact on data, system integrity, and availability is rated high. A researcher write-up from Upwind describes the same bypass of the allowUnsafePack guard. Two packages from the steveukx/git-js project are affected. These are simple-git below 4.1.0 and @simple-git/argv-parser below 3.0.0. The parser package holds the checks that spot dangerous flags, so both need updating together. The maintainers shipped the fix in the simple-git 4.1.0 release on 16 November. The notes say allowUnsafePack now blocks –exec for every command except rebase. The release also adds allowConfig and strict options. It adds a git.cmd helper too, which treats every inserted value as untrusted data that cannot add options or change settings. The maintainers thanked 18 contributors for submitting CVE proposals that shaped these changes. NVD published the record on 22 November. This is not the first time simple-git has had trouble with argument handling. In 2022, CVE-2022-24433 showed that injecting Git options into fetch() could run commands. Earlier this year, CVE-2026-28292 used a missing case-insensitive regex flag to get around older fixes. The library sees more than 12 million weekly npm downloads. Another advisory, CVE-2026-6951 , covered an incomplete fix that blocked -c but not –config. The pattern is clear. Block lists of bad options are hard to keep complete, because Git accepts many ways to write the same option. Upgrade to simple-git 4.1.0 and @simple-git/argv-parser 3.0.0 or later. Then run npm ls simple-git to find copies pulled in by other packages, since many projects use it indirectly. Developers should also stop passing raw user input into listRemote() or raw(). Checking values against a fixed list of allowed repository URLs and branch names is a safer habit. Running the app as a low-rights user adds another layer of protection. Node.js libraries that run system commands have been a steady source of serious problems. A command injection flaw in the systeminformation package followed the same idea of unchecked input reaching a shell. Teams should also keep strict control of their dependencies, as shown when the Keyv package compromise reached millions of weekly installs. Use lockfiles, run npm ci in build systems, and review updates before they ship. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting Cisco Expressway Vulnerability to Gain Full Root Access
items.summary: Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability in Cisco Expressway that lets remote attackers run operating system commands with root privileges. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20, 2026, after finding evidence of active exploitation. Cisco says there is no workaround and urges customers to upgrade. Cisco first disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 and assigned it a severity score of 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its original coverage of the Cisco Expressway vulnerability , fixed software was available before CISA confirmed exploitation. The federal patch deadline was November 23. The catalog entry also directs agencies to follow CISA’s requirements for checking affected devices for signs of compromise. Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Grants Root Access The vulnerability affects the database service used by clustered Expressway devices. Cisco’s security advisory points to persistent cookies and a failure to check client certificates even when TLS verification is enabled for clustering. An attacker who has the required cookies and can reach the affected device over the network can run commands without a normal login. Those commands run as root, the highest level of access on the underlying operating system. Both Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) are affected, whether deployed as virtual machines or physical appliances. For this specific vulnerability, the device must run an affected software release and be part of a cluster. That distinction matters when checking an inventory: the product name and software version alone do not establish whether a device is exposed. The risk can extend beyond the first device. In a case covered by Cyber Security News , researchers at F6 reported that attackers compromised two internet-facing Expressway devices at one organization and reached two internal cluster members through one of them. Security teams should therefore check internal members of an affected cluster, even if those devices are not directly reachable from the internet. Cisco Expressway Fixed Versions Cisco lists X15.5.20 as the first fixed release for customers running X15.5.3 and earlier. Customers on X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. The update also includes Cisco’s October Expressway security hardening fixes , which address several other vulnerabilities. Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the root access vulnerability. Cisco Expressway release Affected products and configuration First fixed release or required action X14 and earlier Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E, physical or virtual, when configured in a cluster Migrate to a fixed release. Cisco does not list a fix in the X14 release train. Administrators should verify the installed version on every cluster member after upgrading. If a vulnerable device was reachable from the internet, preserve available logs and review activity on both the exposed device and its internal peers. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20, 2026, after finding evidence of active exploitation. Cisco says there is no workaround and urges customers to upgrade.

Cisco first disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 and assigned it a severity score of 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its original coverage of the Cisco Expressway vulnerability, fixed software was available before CISA confirmed exploitation. The federal patch deadline was November 23. The catalog entry also directs agencies to follow CISA’s requirements for checking affected devices for signs of compromise.

Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Grants Root Access

The vulnerability affects the database service used by clustered Expressway devices. Cisco’s security advisory points to persistent cookies and a failure to check client certificates even when TLS verification is enabled for clustering.

An attacker who has the required cookies and can reach the affected device over the network can run commands without a normal login. Those commands run as root, the highest level of access on the underlying operating system.

Both Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) are affected, whether deployed as virtual machines or physical appliances. For this specific vulnerability, the device must run an affected software release and be part of a cluster. That distinction matters when checking an inventory: the product name and software version alone do not establish whether a device is exposed.

The risk can extend beyond the first device. In a case covered by Cyber Security News, researchers at F6 reported that attackers compromised two internet-facing Expressway devices at one organization and reached two internal cluster members through one of them.

Security teams should therefore check internal members of an affected cluster, even if those devices are not directly reachable from the internet.

Cisco Expressway Fixed Versions

Cisco lists X15.5.20 as the first fixed release for customers running X15.5.3 and earlier. Customers on X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. The update also includes Cisco’s October Expressway security hardening fixes, which address several other vulnerabilities. Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the root access vulnerability.

Cisco Expressway releaseAffected products and configurationFirst fixed release or required actionX14 and earlierCisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E, physical or virtual, when configured in a clusterMigrate to a fixed release. Cisco does not list a fix in the X14 release train. X15.5.3 and earlier in the X15 release trainCisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E, physical or virtual, when configured in a clusterUpgrade to X15.5.20, the first fixed release listed by Cisco.

Administrators should verify the installed version on every cluster member after upgrading. If a vulnerable device was reachable from the internet, preserve available logs and review activity on both the exposed device and its internal peers. The update closes the vulnerability, but it cannot tell you whether someone already used it.

items.title: Know the identity behind the role: Authorize and audit with trusted identity propagation
items.summary: Today, AWS is making it easier to grant access and audit activity based on the user or workload (a non-human caller, such as an application, service, or an automated workflow) behind an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role. Trusted identity propagation (TIP) carries the identity of the user or workload with each AWS request, so you can grant permissions to that user or workload and trace its actions in AWS CloudTrail . Until now, TIP was available only for users who access AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center . We’ve extended TIP to IAM federation and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere , making it work for users and workloads that federate directly into IAM roles or use X.509 certificates to obtain AWS credentials. We’ve also made TIP simpler to use with IAM Identity Center. This post explains how TIP works and what’s new with this launch. It then shows two examples of how TIP improves auditability and access control based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. The post ends with how to get started depending on your preferred federation path into AWS. How trusted identity propagation works Customers have told us they want to control access to AWS resources and audit activity based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. Today, access control decisions apply to the role, and CloudTrail attributes each action to the role session. To give two users or workloads different access, you either create a separate role or share one role and write policies that check session attributes. Separate roles lead to role proliferation. Session attributes carry across role sessions only when you grant additional permissions, and the session doesn’t record who set each attribute. TIP addresses this gap by attaching identity context from a trusted source, such as your identity provider (IdP), to the role session at the time of credential issuance. This identity context identifies the user or workload behind a request and can include optional claims for the session, such as a risk score or a continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) workflow name. Trusted sources include external SAML or OIDC IdPs configured for IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and X.509 certificates configured for IAM Roles Anywhere. After AWS attaches identity context to a role session, the context can’t be changed for the lifetime of the session. This approach gives IAM policies and audit records a stable reference to the user or workload behind each request. The context also carries forward to supported downstream requests. When a TIP session (a role session that carries identity context) assumes another role, AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) carries the context into the new role session. Similarly, when an AWS service makes a downstream request on your behalf, the request uses forward access sessions (FAS) , and the FAS credentials carry the identity context from your session. Note: TIP context propagates to a new role session only when the target role is in the account where the identity provider is configured, or if the target role is in another account in the same AWS organization. To learn how account and organization boundaries determine TIP context propagation, see Understand where TIP context propagates in the IAM User Guide. Figure 1 shows how this flow works end-to-end. A user or workload obtains AWS credentials through one of three paths. With IAM federation, the source is a SAML assertion or OIDC token for a user or workload. With IAM Identity Center, the source is the username that IAM Identity Center receives from your identity source. With IAM Roles Anywhere, the source is an X.509 certificate for a user or workload. AWS validates the source and attaches identity context to the role session. That context stays with the session’s requests, whether the session calls an AWS service directly, assumes another role, or causes an AWS service to make downstream requests through FAS. IAM policies then evaluate the identity context to authorize requests, as the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket policy example later in this post shows, and AWS CloudTrail records it, as the AWS Lambda example shows. With IAM outbound identity federation, the session can also request a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries identity context to an external service. Figure 1: How TIP carries identity information into authorization and audit workflows AWS represents the identity context carried in a TIP session through three groups of context keys. The following table summarizes their purpose and points to the corresponding documentation. For details about what these context keys contain and when they appear in a TIP session, see TIP context keys in IAM policies . Context keys Purpose aws:OriginIdentity/* Identifies the user or workload that started the request and the source that issued its identity. aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* Carries optional claims from your IdP, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name. Available only for IAM federation. aws:IdentityCenterInstanceArn and aws:IdentityStoreArn Identifies the IAM Identity Center instance and identity store behind a session. If you use IAM Identity Center permission sets or IAM account access manager, you can use these keys in IAM policy conditions. For example, you can allow access only to workforce users from a specific instance. Table 1: TIP context key categories and what they represent. aws:OriginIdentity/* is the common namespace for identity information from IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere. Across all three paths, aws:OriginIdentity/Subject identifies the user or workload that started the request, aws:OriginIdentity/SubjectType indicates whether the request was started by a user or workload, and aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer identifies the source that issued the identity. For IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, aws:OriginIdentity/FederatedProviderArn also contains the Amazon Resource Name ARN) of the IAM IdP or IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchor that authenticated the identity. IAM policies can evaluate TIP context keys when those keys are present in the request. CloudTrail records identity context in the userIdentity element of events. The userIdentity.onBehalfOf section records the user or workload identity from aws:OriginIdentity context keys, and the userIdentity.transactionContext section records IdP claims from aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider context keys. For field definitions and examples see Logging TIP activity with AWS CloudTrail . Key benefits of trusted identity propagation TIP gives you the following benefits for authorizing and auditing access based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. Audit by identity, not only by role – CloudTrail records the user or workload behind each request. Authorize based on who’s asking – IAM policies can grant or restrict access based on the user or workload, or on optional claims from your IdP, such as a risk score. This gives you precise access control for each session. Rely on identity you can trust – AWS attaches identity context from a trusted source when it issues credentials. That context can’t be changed for the life of the session, and it carries forward when the session assumes another role or an AWS service makes requests on your behalf. Use one model across federation paths – IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere share the same core aws:OriginIdentity context keys, so you write policies and review CloudTrail consistently across more than 250 supported AWS services . Across supported workflows, identity context propagates without adding the sts:SetContext permission to role trust policies. What’s new with this launch This launch extends TIP to IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, and simplifies TIP in IAM Identity Center. You can also share identity context with services outside AWS through IAM outbound identity federation. AWS IAM Identity Center – TIP already allows AWS applications integrated with IAM Identity Center, such as AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 Access Grants , to audit user activity and control access based on the user’s identity. When you enable the simplified experience, Identity Center adds a username, an identifier from your identity source, alongside the system-generated identity store user ID. This identity information is carried consistently across all access paths, including application access, account access through IAM Identity Center permission sets, and IAM account access manager. With this launch, you can now use the propagated username, mapped to the aws:OriginIdentity/Subject context key, in IAM policy conditions and view it in CloudTrail events. For more information, see Simplified experience for trusted identity propagation . IAM federation – For users and workloads that use direct SAML or OIDC federation into IAM roles , you choose the SAML assertion field or OIDC token claim that identifies the user or workload, and TIP attaches it to the role session. You can also map optional SAML attributes or OIDC claims, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name, into aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys. TIP is turned on by default for new IAM IdPs, and you can turn it on for existing providers. For more information, see TIP for IAM Federation . IAM Roles Anywhere – For users and workloads outside AWS that use X.509 certificates with IAM Roles Anywhere, TIP attaches the identity from the certificate to the role session. After IAM Roles Anywhere validates the certificate against the configured trust anchor, AWS sets aws:OriginIdentity/Subject to the certificate’s Subject common name by default, or to its URI Subject Alternative Name. TIP is turned on by default for new IAM Roles Anywhere profiles, and you can turn it on for existing profiles. For details, see Trusted identity propagation with IAM Roles Anywhere . IAM outbound identity federation – A TIP session can now use the AWS STS GetWebIdentityToken API operation to request a signed JSON Web Toke that includes TIP session identity context for an external service. The external service validates the token and determines how to use the information. For details, see Federating AWS identities to external services . Use identity context for auditability and access control The following examples demonstrate two core benefits of TIP: auditability—tracing actions back to the user or workload—and access control based on that identity. In the first example, AnyCompany uses identity context logged in CloudTrail to identify the GitHub Actions workflow run that deployed new code to a production AWS Lambda function. In the second, AnyCompany uses an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket policy that grants read access only to low-risk sessions initiated from a specific IdP. Trace a Lambda deployment to its GitHub Actions run This example shows how TIP improves auditability: identity context in CloudTrail identifies the workload, and the specific workflow run, behind an action taken with a shared role. AnyCompany stores the backend code for its payment-processing application in the anycompany/payments-api GitHub repository. A code change merged into the repository’s main branch triggers the GitHub Actions workflow defined in .github/workflows/deploy.yml . The workflow uses GitHub OIDC federation to assume a shared CICDDeployRole role, then calls the Lambda UpdateFunctionCode API operation to deploy the new code to the production payments-api-prod function. CloudTrail records this operation as an UpdateFunctionCode20150331v2 management event. Before TIP, the CloudTrail event shows that the CICDDeployRole/GitHubActions role session updated payments-api-prod . It doesn’t identify the GitHub repository, workflow file, or workflow run that performed the update. Investigators must match the event timestamp with GitHub records to find the responsible workflow run. Figure 2: How TIP enables attribution of a production Lambda code update to the GitHub Actions run that performed it AnyCompany enables TIP on its GitHub OIDC IdP. It maps the GitHub OIDC token subject to aws:OriginIdentity/Subject , configures aws:OriginIdentity/SubjectType as workload, and maps the repository , workflow_ref , and run_id claims into aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys. The resulting role session identifies the workload and carries the information needed to trace the deployment to its GitHub Actions run. With TIP, the CloudTrail management event for the Lambda UpdateFunctionCode API operation on payments-api-prod now contains the workload and workflow information: { "eventSource": "lambda.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "UpdateFunctionCode20150331v2", "recipientAccountId": "111122223333", "requestParameters": { "functionName": "payments-api-prod" }, "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/CICDDeployRole/GitHubActions", "onBehalfOf": { "federatedProviderArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com", "subject": "repo:anycompany/payments-api:environment:production", "subjectType": "workload", "issuer": "token.actions.githubusercontent.com" }, "transactionContext": { "IdentityProvider": { "repository": "anycompany/payments-api", "workflow_ref": "anycompany/payments-api/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@refs/heads/main", "run_id": "19283746550" } } } } An investigator can now see that GitHub Actions run 19283746550 from the anycompany/payments-api repository updated the production payments-api-prod function through the deploy.yml workflow. The shared role, its trust policy, and its permissions remain unchanged. TIP adds workload and workflow attribution to the existing deployment model. Authorize access based on session risk This example shows how TIP supports access control: an Amazon S3 bucket policy uses a runtime risk signal from an IdP to decide, per session, whether a user of a shared role can read sensitive data. AnyCompany’s workforce users federate to AWS through an OIDC IdP and use a shared DataAccessRole to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. AnyCompany configures its IdP to evaluate each authentication and add a numeric risk score, from 0 to 100, to the OIDC token as a custom claim. AnyCompany enables TIP on the IAM OIDC IdP and maps the riskScore claim to the aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/riskScore context key. During federation, AWS validates the token and attaches the mapped riskScore value to the role session. AWS derives aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer from the iss (issuer) claim in the OIDC token. Before TIP, a bucket policy that grants access to DataAccessRole gives every user who assumes the role the same access, regardless of how risky their authentication was. With TIP, an S3 bucket policy can evaluate both the IdP that issued the token and the risk score carried in the session. The following policy grants read access only when the expected IdP (issuer) issued the identity, and the current session has a risk score of 30 or lower. The issuer condition prevents a riskScore value from another IdP from satisfying the policy. Figure 3: How an S3 bucket policy uses trusted identity context to make a per-session access decision Note: This policy example is for the IAM federation access path. Mapping SAML attributes or OIDC claims to optional aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys is available only for IAM federation. Amazon S3 bucket policy using trusted runtime context { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowLowRiskSensitiveDataRead", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DataAccessRole" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/restricted/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer": "idp.example.com" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/riskScore": "30" } } } ] } The policy has two conditions: the identity must come from idp.example.com, and the session’s risk score must be 30 or lower. A low-risk session from idp.example.com satisfies both conditions. A session with a risk score above 30, a missing risk score, or a different issuer doesn’t receive access from this policy. The risk score remains fixed for the lifetime of the role session, so choose a session duration appropriate for the sensitivity of the access. Additional considerations Missing TIP context keys. A TIP context key is missing when the session carries no identity context or the request goes to an AWS service that doesn’t support TIP. To prevent an Allow statement from granting access when a required key is missing, use operators without IfExists , such as StringEquals or NumericLessThanEquals , as the preceding bucket policy does. Avoid operators such as StringEqualsIfExists in an Allow statement because they evaluate to true when the key is missing. In a Deny statement, add IfExists when the Deny should also apply if the key is missing. Such a Deny also applies to requests sent to AWS services that don’t support TIP, so confirm service support before adding TIP conditions. For more information, see Condition operators . TIP conditions with cached AWS KMS data keys. Some AWS services, such as Amazon SQS , reuse cached AWS KMS data keys across requests from different sessions of the same IAM role, because the cache key is based on the role and does not include TIP context. When an AWS service reuses a cached data key, it does not send a new authorization request to AWS KMS, so AWS KMS does not evaluate the later session’s TIP context. If you use TIP context to control access to encrypted data, enforce the TIP conditions in the policy for the encrypted resource, such as an Amazon S3 bucket policy, rather than relying only on the AWS KMS key policy. For more information, see AWS KMS guidance for cached data keys . Choose your TIP approach and get started Your first step to getting started with TIP depends on how your users and workloads obtain AWS credentials. Use the following table to find the TIP option for your use case and get started. Use case TIP option How to start Centrally managed workforce access IAM Identity Center All IAM Identity Center instances can upgrade to the simplified experience for TIP. Before you upgrade, review the considerations for the simplified experience. For more information, see Simplified experience for trusted identity propagation . Direct SAML or OIDC federation into IAM roles IAM federation New IAM IdPs have TIP turned on by default. For an existing IdP, turn on TIP on that provider, then map the claim that identifies the user or workload, and any optional claims your policies need, to TIP context keys. For more information see TIP for IAM Federation . X.509-based access for users and workloads outside AWS IAM Roles Anywhere New profiles have TIP turned on by default. For an existing profile, enable TIP on the profile. For details, see Trusted identity propagation with IAM Roles Anywhere . Conclusion With this launch, TIP carries the identity of the user or workload from a trusted identity source into the role session for IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere. You can grant access based on the user or workload making the request and use CloudTrail to trace actions across more than 250 supported AWS services back to that identity. This gives you a consistent authorization and audit model across federation paths, without creating a separate role for every identity or adding the sts:SetContext permission to role trust policies. To get started, find your federation path in the preceding table and follow the steps in the How to start column. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . In her free time, she enjoys wreck diving and traveling around the world. Rishi Tripathy Rishi is a Principal Product Manager on the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) team. He focuses on access control mechanisms that help enterprises secure their AWS environments at scale. He is passionate about building security primitives that are straightforward to adopt and hard to misconfigure. Songzhi Liu Songzhi is a Principal Big Data Architect with the AWS Identity Solutions team. In this role, he collaborates closely with AWS customers and cross-functional teams to design and implement scalable data architectures, focusing on integrating big data and machine learning solutions to enhance identity awareness within the AWS ecosystem. Shweta Motwani Shweta is a Senior Product Manager on the AWS IAM Identity Center team, focused on increasing identity awareness across AWS services to allow for improved auditing and access control. Shweta joined AWS in 2017 and has previously worked as a product manager in Amazon EBS, driving Provisioned IOPS growth and with software partners in the AWS Partner Network.
